blocks.x: Algebraic equation A mathematical statement that relates two algebraic expressions with an equal sign, where one or both expressions involve variables, numbers, and binary operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division or exponents). General form: expression 1 = expression 2.
Domain of a variable The set of possible values the variable can take for the equation or expression to make sense and be valid — i.e. the set of all values for which it is defined.
Solution set / root The set of values of the variable that satisfy the equation. Each member of the solution set is called a solution or a root of the equation.
Types of equations in this module

c: ax + b = 0 (one var.), ax + by = c (two var.)

blocks.x: Domain, solution sets, and the two standard forms of a linear equation — solved by substitution and elimination.
Find the domain of x in: 1x = 2x−3

items: 1The left side is undefined whenever its denominator is zero.x = 0 makes 1/x undefined
2The right side is undefined whenever its denominator is zero.x − 3 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 makes 2/(x−3) undefined
3Both values must be excluded from the domain; every other real number is valid.

blocks.x: Domain: x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 0 and x ≠ 3
By contrast, the domain of x in 2x − 4 = 0 is simply ℝ (all real numbers) — there is no denominator or root to restrict it.

Linear / first-degree equation
Any equation that can be written in the form ax + b = 0, a ≠ 0. Examples: 5x − 9 = 0, 7x − 10 = 0.

items: 1Isolate the term containing x by adding 9 to both sides.5x = 9
2Divide both sides by the coefficient of x.x = 9 ÷ 5

blocks.x: A linear equation is one in which the highest degree of the variable(s) is 1; its graph is a straight line. The standard form is ax + by = c, a, b ≠ 0, where a and b are the coefficients of x and y, and c is the constant term. Each solution corresponds to an ordered pair (x, y) — a point in the coordinate plane. Such systems are solved by substitution, elimination, or the graphical method.
Solve for one variable in one equation, then substitute that expression into the other equation.
Solve by substitution: x − y = 3 and x + 2y = −3

items: 1Make x the subject of the first equation.x − y = 3 ⇒ x = y + 3
2Substitute x = y + 3 into the second equation.(y + 3) + 2y = −3

blocks.x: Eliminate one variable by adding the two equations together, or subtracting one from the other.

items: 1The y-terms are opposite in sign, so add the equations to eliminate y.(x + 2y) + (3x − 2y) = 4 + 2 ⇒ 4x = 6
3Substitute x = 1.5 into x + 2y = 4 and solve for y.1.5 + 2y = 4 ⇒ 2y = 2.5 ⇒ y = 1.25
1The y-terms match, so subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate y.(2x + 3y) − (x + 3y) = 7 − 4 ⇒ x = 3
2Substitute x = 3 into x + 3y = 4 and solve for y.3 + 3y = 4 ⇒ 3y = 1 ⇒ y = 1/3

blocks.x: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), solved four ways: factoring, square roots, completing the square, and the general formula.
If ax² + bx + c = 0 can be written as the product of two linear factors, the equation can be solved quickly by factoring.

items: 1Move all terms to the left side.x² − 6x + 5 + 4 = 0 ⇒ x² − 6x + 9 = 0

blocks.x: If a quadratic can be written as a perfect square equal to a constant — i.e. ax² + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) — it can be solved using the square root approach.

items: 2Take the square root of both sides.x = ±√(3/2)
2Take the square root of both sides.x = ±√9

blocks.x: Trial exercise — solve by square root approach
Transform ax² + bx + c = 0 into the form (x + A)² = B. To complete the square of x² + bx, add the square of half the coefficient of x: (b/2)². Thus x² + bx + (b/2)² = (x + b/2)².
Example 1 — Solve x² + 6x − 2 = 0 by completing the square

items: 1Move the constant to the right side.x² + 6x = 2
4Write the left side as a perfect square.(x + 3)² = 11

Solution by the general quadratic formula

Quadratic formula
For ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0: x = −b ± √(b² − 4ac)2a
Solve 6x² + 7x + 2 = 0 by the general quadratic method
Solve x² − 6x + 3 = 0 using the general quadratic formula
The expression b² − 4ac in the quadratic formula is called the discriminant. It determines the type and nature of the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0:

c: A pair of complex conjugate roots

blocks.x: Degree, zeros and factors of a polynomial, and the two standard ways to divide one polynomial by another.

Polynomial P(x) A function of the form P(x) = Σk=1n akxk, an ≠ 0 is called an nth-degree polynomial. The degree is the highest power/exponent present in the polynomial; a, b, c, d are constants while x is the variable, so P(x) is a polynomial in x.
For instance f(x) = ax² + bx + c is a second-degree polynomial, commonly called a quadratic function, while f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d is a third-degree polynomial — a cubic function.
Zero of a polynomial P(x), or root of P(x) = 0

Zero / root / factor A number a is a zero of the polynomial P(x), or a root/solution of P(x) = 0, if P(a) = 0. When this holds, x − a is a factor of P(x). Similarly, if P(−a) = 0, then −a is a root of P(x) = 0 and x + a is a factor of P(x).
Arrange the dividend and the divisor in descending powers of the variable, always inserting a zero coefficient for any missing term.

items: 1Divide the leading term of the dividend by the leading term of the divisor; multiply and subtract.4x³ ÷ 2x = 2x² ⇒ 2x²(2x−3) = 4x³−6x² ⇒ remainder so far: 6x² − 3x + 5
2Repeat with the new leading term.6x² ÷ 2x = 3x ⇒ 3x(2x−3) = 6x²−9x ⇒ remainder so far: 6x + 5
3Repeat once more until the remainder's degree is less than the divisor's.6x ÷ 2x = 3 ⇒ 3(2x−3) = 6x−9 ⇒ final remainder: 14

blocks.x: More practice — divide by long division

To divide P(x) by x − a: arrange the dividend's coefficients in descending powers (inserting zero for missing powers); solve x − a = 0 for the divisor value a; bring down the first coefficient; multiply it by a and add to the second coefficient; repeat this multiply-and-add process across every coefficient. The last number in the resulting row is the remainder; the numbers before it are the coefficients of the quotient, which has degree one less than P(x).
Divide 2x⁴ + 3x³ − x − 5 by x + 2 (synthetic division, a = −2)

items: 1List coefficients in descending order, inserting 0 for the missing x² term.2, 3, 0, −1, −5 | a = −2
2Bring down 2. Multiply by a, add to next coefficient — repeat across the row.2 → 2(−2)+3=−1 → −1(−2)+0=2 → 2(−2)+(−1)=−5 → −5(−2)+(−5)=5
1List coefficients in descending order, inserting 0 for the missing x⁴ and x² terms.4, 0, −30, 0, −50, −2 | a = −3

blocks.x: ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 (a ≠ 0) has three possible roots — real or complex — found here by factorization and the factor theorem.

Cubic equation Any equation of the form ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0, a ≠ 0. Cubic equations have three possible roots, which may be real or complex. Roots may be found by factorization, graphing, or other formulas such as Cardano's Formula.

items: 1Group the first two terms and the last two terms.x³ − 4x² − 9x + 36 = 0

blocks.x: Unlike the previous example, x³ − 7x − 6 = 0 cannot be factorized easily since its coefficients share no common factors. Instead, the factor theorem is used: guess and check values of x to find a zero of the expression.

items: 2Since the expression equals zero, (x + 1) is a linear factor.
3Divide x³ − 7x − 6 by (x + 1) to get the quadratic factor.x³ − 7x − 6 = (x + 1)(x² − x − 6)
